For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the street's name on the back of each. This spring white reflective letters on green metal replaced them.

The change began at a town meeting in January, where residents voted for new signs to match the ones on the county roads. When the two Gates came down in February, each had the other's name pencilled on its back. Arthur Venn, who drove the town's ambulance for thirty years, laughed when he heard and said he had known about the swap since his first night shift. Both lanes end in the same square, so he had always simply taken whichever one was nearer.

Dora Pask, the town clerk, turned the two boards over herself, struck the word Upper on her list, and wrote Lower above it. Marrow, it seems, had painted both Gates on the same afternoon in his first week and carried them out together. Visiting drivers who mistook one Gate for the other arrived in the same square anyway. The county's rule on reflective letters covers only county roads, so the residents' vote was the whole of the reason for the change. It is hard to picture a happier mix-up than two boards hidden in plain sight on each other's lanes for four decades, with every driver arriving where they meant to go.

Only three boards in town showed any rot at their edges. After a week in storage at the depot shed, each old board went to the longest-serving resident of its street. The new signs carry the county's plain letters, made larger at the post office's request, and they went up on the right posts.

I laughed out loud when I read the council's notice, and again last week when Nora Hale of Lower Gate showed me her board hanging in her front hall, the word Upper facing the door.

passage:
The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. My mother had asked her in June to find me something to do besides lie on the porch, and the next morning a spare veil was waiting on our back steps. Mrs. Pellow's two hives sat on the roof of her shed, a spot she had chosen to keep the bees above the fence along Tamsin Lane, and she had built both of them herself long ago, a summer's work.

By July I could lift a frame without flinching, and every morning Mrs. Pellow climbed the ladder onto the shed roof beside me. Late that month a swarm poured off the roof, passed over the lilac by the back gate, and settled on the fence along Tamsin Lane, above the walk to the pool, where I found it at noon. My mother came from the clothesline by our back steps to turn people back, while Mrs. Pellow fetched a box from under the eaves of the shed and set the swarm beneath the pear tree by her kitchen.

The pitch of that roof was far too steep for hives, and on July afternoons the sun beat on the boxes until the wax went soft and the bees hung out of the entrances in sheets. Every inspection meant carrying frames down the ladder and back up again, which took twice as long as it should have and left the bees quick to sting.

In August we took away the full frames and spun out the honey. She sold it on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. From our porch I could hear the sound of the hives over the traffic on the lane, and in winter she left them up on the roof, where the wind off the hill struck them full on.

Hives belong on level ground in afternoon shade, and hers should have stood behind the shed, where the lilac would have kept the sun off them and nobody would have needed a ladder. She kept the hives on that roof every summer afterwards.

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the tellers at the bank on Mill Street pull down the shutters, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead in a dark, turning cloud. Then the last bus passes the school gates, and the whole cloud pours down into the chimney like smoke running backwards; by the time the streetlights on the hill come on, the sky is clear.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit the school's furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed, eleven years ago. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds. Of all his stories, the one he tells most often is about that furnace.

It was the first September after the school closed. Walking home past Linden Row at dusk, Reyburn saw a dark plume over the chimney, ran to the boiler room with a fire bucket, and flung open the furnace door to find the grate cold and swifts pattering down the flue. He tells it laughing, and he always slaps his knee at the part with the bucket. When the storm two winters ago put a crack near the chimney's top, the council voted to mend it and keep it standing, just as Reyburn had said it would, and the masons did the work in lime mortar rather than cheap cement, rough as the old brick.

I laughed out loud the first evening I saw it myself: a chimney that has burned nothing for eleven years, drawing a cloud of smoke down into itself.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand cold until they return in May. Until they go, every clear evening the old chimney smokes in reverse over the schoolyard, and I stand at the gate grinning up at it.
